content: Pelvic organ prolapse is a prevalent condition, with approximately 50% of women who have given birth experiencing some degree of prolapse. Women with this condition may present with a range of pelvic floor symptoms. Treatment options for pelvic organ prolapse include surgical interventions, mechanical devices, and conservative management strategies. Conservative management, which is often employed for mild to moderate cases, typically involves lifestyle modifications and pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT). This document is an updated Cochrane review, originally published in 2004 and updated in 2006, that evaluates the effects of conservative management for the prevention or treatment of pelvic organ prolapse compared to no treatment or other interventions such as surgery or mechanical devices. The objective of this review was to assess the impact of conservative management, including physical and lifestyle interventions, on pelvic organ prolapse. The review compared these approaches to no treatment or alternative treatment options. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Incontinence Group Specialised Trials Register, EMBASE, CINAHL, PEDro, and others, up to May 2010. Reference lists of pertinent articles were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized and quasi-randomized trials involving women with pelvic organ prolapse, where at least one arm of the trial included a physical or lifestyle intervention. Two reviewers independently assessed the trials for inclusion and methodological quality. Data extraction was performed by the lead reviewer and cross-checked by another reviewer. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion. The data were processed in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. Six trials were included in this review, three of which were new additions. Four of the trials were small, with fewer than 25 participants per arm, and two trials exhibited a moderate to high risk of bias. Four trials compared PFMT as a treatment for prolapse against a control group, involving a total of 857 women. Two trials examined the use of PFMT as an adjunct to surgery, comparing outcomes between surgery alone and surgery supplemented with PFMT, involving 118 women. In the comparison of PFMT versus control, two of the four trials had a significant risk of bias. Prolapse symptoms and treatment outcomes, which were primary outcomes, were measured differently across the three trials that reported these outcomes. All three trials indicated greater symptom improvement in the PFMT group compared to the control group. Data pooled from two trials suggested that PFMT increased the likelihood of improvement in prolapse stage by 17% compared to no PFMT. Two trials that assessed pelvic floor muscle function reported better function or improvement in the PFMT group compared to the control group, although the measurements were not blinded. Regarding urinary outcomes, two out of three trials reported favorable results for the PFMT group, including improvements in urodynamics, symptom frequency, and symptom bother. One trial assessed bowel outcomes and found that the PFMT group experienced less frequent and bothersome symptoms compared to the control group. In the comparison of PFMT supplementing surgery versus surgery alone, both trials were small and did not measure prolapse-specific outcomes. Findings related to pelvic floor muscle function were inconsistent between the two trials. One trial found no difference in muscle strength between groups, while the other reported stronger muscles in the PFMT group. Similarly, urinary outcomes were contradictory. One trial found no difference in symptom score changes between groups, whereas the other trial reported greater improvement in urinary symptoms and a reduction in diurnal frequency in the PFMT group compared to the control group. The authors concluded that there is emerging evidence supporting the positive effects of PFMT on prolapse symptoms and severity. The largest and most rigorous trial to date suggests that six months of supervised PFMT can lead to anatomical and symptomatic improvements immediately after the intervention. However, further research is needed to evaluate the mediumand long-term effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of PFMT, particularly at varying intensities, for symptomatic prolapse. Additionally, a large trial is required to determine the utility of combining PFMT with surgery. Other comparisons, such as those involving lifestyle interventions or trials aimed at prolapse prevention, have not yet been addressed and warrant further investigation.
